title: English Quantifiers Practice Questions
description: 50 practice questions based on the English Quantifiers Study Guide.

questions.question: Which of the following words is an uncountable noun?
questions.explanation: 'Information' is an uncountable noun and cannot be made plural directly.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) She gave me three good advices.
B) She gave me an advice.
C) She gave me three pieces of advice.
D) She gave me three piece of advice.
questions.explanation: Uncountable nouns like 'advice' use measure words like 'pieces of' to show quantity.

questions.question: Select the incorrect expression:
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and cannot take the plural form 'furnitures'.

questions.question: Which noun can be used with the article 'a' or 'an'?
questions.explanation: 'Student' is a countable singular noun, so it takes 'a'.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'The technician installed three new ___ of equipment in the lab.'
questions.explanation: Both 'pieces' and 'items' can be used as counters for uncountable nouns like equipment.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'I bought ___ apples at the store.'
questions.explanation: 'Some' is used in affirmative statements with plural countable nouns.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'We do not have ___ money left for expenses.'
questions.explanation: 'Any' is standard in negative statements.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'Would you like ___ coffee?'
questions.explanation: 'Some' is used in questions when offering something.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'You can choose ___ book you like from the shelf.'
questions.explanation: 'Any' in an affirmative sentence can mean 'it does not matter which'.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct for a question asking for permission/request?
options: A) Could I have any water, please?
B) Could I have some water, please?
C) Could I have many water, please?
D) Could I have few water, please?
questions.explanation: 'Some' is used in requests where a positive answer is expected.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'How ___ students are enrolled in the course?'
questions.explanation: 'Many' is used with plural countable nouns like 'students'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'There isn't ___ water left in the container.'
questions.explanation: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns like 'water' in negative sentences.

questions.question: Which option is most natural in informal affirmative sentences?
options: A) I have much work to do today.
B) I have a lot of work to do today.
C) I have many work to do today.
D) I have few work to do today.
questions.explanation: In informal affirmative sentences, 'a lot of' is more natural than 'much'.

questions.question: Which context often uses 'much' in affirmative statements?
questions.explanation: 'Much' is common in formal or academic contexts (e.g., 'Much research has been done').

questions.question: Identify the incorrect sentence:
options: A) She doesn't have many friends.
B) There are much opportunities available.
C) How much money do you need?
D) We don't have much time.
questions.explanation: 'Opportunities' is countable plural, so it requires 'many', not 'much'.

questions.category: A Lot of, Lots of, Plenty of
questions.question: 'Plenty of' strictly means:
questions.explanation: 'Plenty of' signifies a comfortable, sufficient quantity or more than enough.

questions.category: A Lot of, Lots of, Plenty of
questions.question: Which quantifier can be used with BOTH countable plural and uncountable nouns?
questions.explanation: 'A lot of' works with both countable plural nouns and uncountable nouns.

questions.category: A Lot of, Lots of, Plenty of
questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'Don't rush, we have ___ time.'
questions.explanation: 'Plenty of' fits uncountable 'time' to indicate more than enough time.

questions.category: A Lot of, Lots of, Plenty of
questions.question: Compare 'a lot of' and 'lots of':
options: A) 'Lots of' is more formal than 'a lot of'.
B) 'Lots of' is slightly more informal than 'a lot of'.
C) 'A lot of' can only be used with countable nouns.
D) They have completely opposite meanings.
questions.explanation: 'Lots of' is slightly more informal than 'a lot of'.

questions.category: A Lot of, Lots of, Plenty of
questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'There were ___ people at the seminar.'
questions.explanation: 'Lots of' modifies plural countable nouns like 'people'.

questions.category: Few, A Few, Little, A Little
questions.question: What is the difference in meaning between 'few' and 'a few'?
options: A) 'Few' has a positive tone; 'a few' has a negative tone.
B) 'Few' means almost none (insufficient); 'a few' means some (sufficient).
C) 'Few' is used with uncountable nouns; 'a few' with countable nouns.
D) There is no grammatical difference.
questions.explanation: 'Few' implies scarcity (negative tone), while 'a few' means a small positive amount.

questions.category: Few, A Few, Little, A Little
questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'He has ___ experience in marketing, so he failed the assessment.'
questions.explanation: 'Experience' is uncountable, and the negative result requires 'little' (almost none).

questions.category: Few, A Few, Little, A Little
questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'We still have ___ minutes before the train leaves.'
questions.explanation: 'Minutes' is countable plural, and having some positive time left calls for 'a few'.

questions.category: Few, A Few, Little, A Little
questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'There is ___ hope of recovery.' (meaning almost no hope)
questions.explanation: 'Hope' is uncountable; 'little hope' means almost no hope.

questions.category: Few, A Few, Little, A Little
questions.question: Which quantifier pairs correctly with uncountable nouns?
questions.explanation: 'Little' and 'a little' modify uncountable nouns.

questions.category: Few, A Few, Little, A Little
questions.question: Select the correct sentence:
options: A) I have a little friends in town.
B) She spoke a little Spanish during the trip.
C) There are little mistakes in your essay.
D) He has a few knowledge about economics.
questions.explanation: 'Spanish' (language) is uncountable, correctly modified by 'a little'.

questions.category: Few, A Few, Little, A Little
questions.question: If I say 'Few people attended the meeting', what does it imply?
options: A) A large group was present.
questions.explanation: 'Few people' emphasizes that attendance was very low.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: '___ student must bring their ID card.'
questions.explanation: 'Every' is followed by a singular countable noun ('student').

questions.question: Which quantifier focuses on members of a group individually?
questions.explanation: 'Each' emphasizes individual items/members separately.

questions.question: Identify the incorrect usage:
options: A) Every students passed the exam.
B) Every student passed the exam.
C) All students passed the exam.
D) Each student received a certificate.
questions.explanation: 'Every' cannot be followed directly by a plural noun ('students').

questions.question: Fill in the blank: '___ the information was stored safely.'
questions.explanation: 'All' can modify uncountable nouns like 'information'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that emphasizes individual difference:
options: C) Each candidate received a different interview score.
questions.explanation: 'Each' highlights individuality in the group.

questions.question: How many items or people do 'both', 'either', and 'neither' refer to?
questions.explanation: These three quantifiers specifically refer to sets of two.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: '___ answer is correct. They are both wrong.'
questions.explanation: 'Neither' means 'not one and not the other'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'You can choose ___ Monday or Tuesday for the interview.'
questions.explanation: 'Either... or' refers to choosing one of two options.

questions.question: What verb form should formally follow 'Neither answer...'?
questions.explanation: 'Neither' takes a singular noun and singular verb in formal grammar.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: '___ of my parents are teachers.'
questions.explanation: 'Both of my parents' refers to the two parents together with a plural verb ('are').

questions.question: Where does 'enough' go when modifying a NOUN?
options: C) At the end of the clause
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes BEFORE a noun (e.g., 'enough money').

questions.question: Where does 'enough' go when modifying an ADJECTIVE?
options: C) At the start of the sentence
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes AFTER an adjective (e.g., 'old enough').

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'There is ___ noise in the hallway.'
questions.explanation: 'Noise' is uncountable, requiring 'too much'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'There are ___ errors in this report.'
questions.explanation: 'Errors' is countable plural, requiring 'too many'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence:
options: A) The room is enough big for us.
B) The room is big enough for us.
C) We have money enough to buy it.
D) She speaks clearly enough not.
questions.explanation: 'Big' is an adjective, so 'enough' follows it.

questions.question: Which sentence contains an ungrammatical double negative?
options: A) I don't have any money.
C) I don't have no money.
D) None of the money was lost.
questions.explanation: 'Don't have no' creates a double negative, which is incorrect in standard English.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'How many questions were answered? ___.'
questions.explanation: 'None' stands alone without a noun in short answers.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: '___ of the students were late.'
questions.explanation: 'None of' is used before determiners + nouns.

questions.question: What verb form follows 'A number of students...'?
questions.explanation: 'A number of' means many and takes a plural verb.

questions.question: What verb form follows 'The number of applicants...'?
questions.explanation: 'The number of' refers to the single numeric total, taking a singular verb.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'A great deal of time ___ spent on research.'
questions.explanation: 'A great deal of' modifies uncountable nouns ('time') and takes a singular verb.

questions.question: When is 'of' required after quantifiers like 'some' or 'many'?
options: A) Before a generic plural noun
B) Before determiners like 'the', 'my', 'these', or pronouns like 'us'
questions.explanation: 'Of' is used when referring to a specific group preceded by determiners/pronouns.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence:
options: A) A lot of information are online.
B) A lot of information is online.
C) A lot of students is present.
questions.explanation: 'A lot of' agreement depends on the noun: 'information' is uncountable, so it takes 'is'.
